scope: All 24 exact systems Teach bodies independently reviewed against each canonical objective, constraints, key and topic prerequisites, and all curriculum exemplars. Every proposed worked result was independently recomputed. The four changed positive-coefficient inequality solution sketches were independently reread; their operation sequence now matches the unchanged answers and lesson concepts. No proposal or live-content approval.

records.canonical_constraints: solve for the variable with coefficient 1; integer solutions

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $x+2y=16$ and $3x+y=18$. Give $(x,y)$.
Solve by substitution: $2x-y=1$ and $x+3y=11$. Give $(x,y)$.
Solve by substitution: $3x+y=2$ and $x-2y=10$. Give $(x,y)$.
Solve by substitution: $x-3y=9$ and $2x+5y=7$. Give $(x,y)$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $x+3y=11$, $4x-y=18$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Selects a coefficient-one variable, substitutes the whole expression with parentheses, back-substitutes, and checks both originals.

records.canonical_constraints: distribute a coefficient over the substituted expression

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $x=2y+3$ and $3x-4y=19$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Distribute after substitution: $3(2y+3)-4y=19$ becomes $2y+9=19$. Solve for $y$, then recover $x$. Check: $(13)=2(5)+3$ and $3(13)-4(5)=19$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $y=3x-2$ and $5x-2y=0$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Substitute and distribute the negative: $5x-2(3x-2)=0$, hence $-x+4=0$. Recover $y$. Check: $(10)=3(4)-2$ and $5(4)-2(10)=0$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $x=7-2y$ and $4x+3y=13$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Expand $4(7-2y)+3y=13$ to $28-5y=13$. Recover $x$ after finding $y$. Check: $(1)=7-2(3)$ and $4(1)+3(3)=13$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $y=-2(x-1)$ and $3x+2y=9$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Substitute the grouped expression: $3x-4(x-1)=9$ gives $-x+4=9$. Evaluate $-2(x-1)$ for $y$. Check: $(12)=-2((-5)-1)$ and $3(-5)+2(12)=9$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $y=4x-5$, $3x-2y=-5$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Explicitly distributes the outside coefficient across every substituted term, including the sign-sensitive negative case.

records.canonical_constraints: subtraction of substituted expressions; integer solutions

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $x+y=3$ and $2x-y=12$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Use $y=3-x$: $2x-(3-x)=12$, so $3x=15$. The minus before the parentheses changes both signs. Check: $(5)+(-2)=3$ and $2(5)-(-2)=12$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $x-2y=-8$ and $3x+y=-3$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Use $x=2y-8$: $3(2y-8)+y=-3$, hence $7y=21$. Recover $x$ including its negative sign. Check: $(-2)-2(3)=-8$ and $3(-2)+(3)=-3$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by substitution: $2x+y=-4$ and $x-3y=5$. Give $(x,y)$.
Solve by substitution: $x+y=-7$ and $-2x+y=2$. Give $(x,y)$.

records.worked_problem: Solve $x+y=15$ and $3x-y=9$ by substituting for the subtracted variable.
records.semantic_reasoning: Protects a subtracted replacement with parentheses and uses both original equations to catch sign errors.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: With y=15-x, 3x-(15-x)=9 gives 4x=24, x=6, y=9; both originals hold.

records.canonical_constraints: coefficients already opposite; integer solutions

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x+y=17$ and $3x-y=13$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Add the equations to cancel $y$: $5x=30$. Subtract $2x$ from $17$ to recover $y$. Check: $2(6)+(5)=17$ and $3(6)-(5)=13$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $x+3y=13$ and $-x+2y=2$. Give $(x,y)$.
Solve by elimination: $3x-2y=16$ and $x+2y=0$. Give $(x,y)$.
Solve by elimination: $-2x-y=1$ and $2x+4y=8$. Give $(x,y)$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $3x + 5y = 21$, $3x - 5y = -9$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses direct addition only when coefficients are already opposites, then recovers and verifies the second coordinate.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Adding 3x+5y=21 and 3x-5y=-9 gives 6x=12, x=2; then y=3.

records.canonical_constraints: matching coefficients; subtract carefully

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $x+3y=19$ and $x+y=9$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Subtract the second equation from the first: $2y=10$. Use $x=9-y$. Check: $(4)+3(5)=19$ and $(4)+(5)=9$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $4x+y=15$ and $x+y=6$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Subtract to cancel $y$: $3x=9$. Use $y=6-x$. Check: $4(3)+(3)=15$ and $(3)+(3)=6$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x-3y=17$ and $2x+y=5$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Subtract the second from the first: $-4y=12$. Use $2x=5-y$. Check: $2(4)-3(-3)=17$ and $2(4)+(-3)=5$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $-x+2y=4$ and $3x+2y=12$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Subtract the first from the second: $4x=8$. Use $2y=4+x$. Check: $-(2)+2(3)=4$ and $3(2)+2(3)=12$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $4x + 3y = 26$, $4x + y = 14$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses whole-equation subtraction when coefficients match and demonstrates careful subtraction of every term.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Subtracting 4x+y=14 from 4x+3y=26 gives 2y=12, y=6 and x=2.

records.canonical_constraints: solutions may include negatives; verify in both equations

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x+y=13$ and $x-y=8$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Add to get $3x=21$. Back-substitute with $y=x-8$ and verify each original equation. Check: $2(7)+(-1)=13$ and $(7)-(-1)=8$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $x+2y=-1$ and $-x+3y=16$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Add to get $5y=15$. Back-substitute with $x=-1-2y$ and verify both equations. Check: $(-7)+2(3)=-1$ and $-(-7)+3(3)=16$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $3x-2y=4$ and $x+2y=-12$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Add to get $4x=-8$. Back-substitute with $2y=-12-x$ and check both equations. Check: $3(-2)-2(-5)=4$ and $(-2)+2(-5)=-12$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $-2x+y=-11$ and $2x+2y=2$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Add to get $3y=-9$. Back-substitute with $2x=2-2y$ and verify both equations. Check: $-2(4)+(-3)=-11$ and $2(4)+2(-3)=2$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $3x + 2y = 4$, $x - 2y = 12$ and check.
records.semantic_reasoning: Allows negative coordinates, back-substitutes, and verifies both original equations after elimination.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Adding 3x+2y=4 and x-2y=12 gives x=4; then y=-4, satisfying both.

records.canonical_constraints: scale to create opposite coefficients; integer solutions

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x+3y=29$ and $x+2y=18$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the second equation by $-2$ and add: $-y=-7$. Recover $x$ from the second equation. Check: $2(4)+3(7)=29$ and $(4)+2(7)=18$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $3x-2y=23$ and $x+y=11$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the second equation by $-3$ and add: $-5y=-10$. Recover $x$ from the second equation. Check: $3(9)-2(2)=23$ and $(9)+(2)=11$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x+y=9$ and $3x-2y=31$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the first equation by $2$ and add: $7x=49$. Recover $y$ from the first equation. Check: $2(7)+(-5)=9$ and $3(7)-2(-5)=31$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $4x+3y=-2$ and $2x-y=-6$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the second equation by $-2$ and add: $5y=10$. Recover $x$ from the second equation. Check: $4(-2)+3(2)=-2$ and $2(-2)-(2)=-6$.

records.worked_problem: Solve $5x+2y=19$ and $3x+y=10$ by scaling one equation to create opposite coefficients.
records.semantic_reasoning: Scales every term and the right side of one equation to create opposite coefficients before adding.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Scaling 3x+y=10 by -2 gives -6x-2y=-20; adding gives x=1, then y=7.

records.canonical_constraints: scale both to match one variable; integer solutions

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x+3y=32$ and $3x+2y=33$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the equations by $3$ and $-2$, respectively, then add: $5y=30$. Recover $x$ from the first equation. Check: $2(7)+3(6)=32$ and $3(7)+2(6)=33$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $3x-4y=2$ and $2x+3y=7$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the equations by $2$ and $-3$, respectively, then add: $-17y=-17$. Recover $x$ from the second equation. Check: $3(2)-4(1)=2$ and $2(2)+3(1)=7$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $4x+3y=-17$ and $3x-2y=-17$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the equations by $2$ and $3$, respectively, then add: $17x=-85$. Recover $y$ from the first equation. Check: $4(-5)+3(1)=-17$ and $3(-5)-2(1)=-17$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $3(x+y)+2y=47$ and $2x-3y=6$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Expand the first equation to $3x+5y=47$. Multiply the equations by $3$ and $5$, respectively, then add: $19x=171$. Recover $y$ from the second equation. Check: $3((9)+(4))+2(4)=47$ and $2(9)-3(4)=6$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $4x+3y=27$, $5x+2y=25$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses a common multiple to scale both complete equations and permits either equal-for-subtraction or opposite-for-addition coefficients.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: After scaling, (15x+6y)-(8x+6y)=75-54 gives x=3; then y=5.

records.canonical_constraints: negative multipliers turn subtraction into addition

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $2x+5y=39$ and $4x+3y=43$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the first equation by $-2$, including its right side. Add: $-7y=-35$. Recover $x$ from the first equation. Check: $2(7)+5(5)=39$ and $4(7)+3(5)=43$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $3x+2y=35$ and $x+4y=35$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the second equation by $-3$, including its right side. Add: $-10y=-70$. Recover $x$ from the second equation. Check: $3(7)+2(7)=35$ and $(7)+4(7)=35$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $-2x+3y=29$ and $-4x+y=23$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the first equation by $-2$: both negative $x$ terms cancel on addition and $-5y=-35$. Recover $x$. Check: $-2(-4)+3(7)=29$ and $-4(-4)+(7)=23$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Solve by elimination: $5x-2y=-9$ and $3x-4y=-11$. Give $(x,y)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiply the first equation by $-2$ and add the second: $-7x=7$. Recover $y$ from the first equation. Check: $5(-1)-2(2)=-9$ and $3(-1)-4(2)=-11$.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $5x+3y=29$, $2x+3y=17$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Shows how a negative multiplier changes every sign and creates addition-based cancellation.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Negating the second equation gives -2x-3y=-17; adding to 5x+3y=29 gives x=4 and y=3.

records.canonical_constraints: elimination ends in a false statement (none) or 0 = 0 (infinite)

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $3x+y=5$ and $6x+2y=14$. Classify the solution set: report infinite and none as yes/no fields, with exactly one yes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Twice the first equation has right side ten. The second has the identical left side but right side fourteen; subtracting gives an impossible equality.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $x=2y+3$ and $2x-4y=6$. Classify the solution set: report infinite and none as yes/no fields, with exactly one yes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Move the vertical term to the left in the first equation, then double both sides. This produces the second equation, so every point of that line solves both.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $y=-3x+4$ and $3x+y=1$. Classify the solution set: report infinite and none as yes/no fields, with exactly one yes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Rearranging the first gives the same left side as the second with right side four. The required right sides differ by three, so no point can satisfy both.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $2x-3y=7$ and $-6x+9y=-21$. Classify the solution set: report infinite and none as yes/no fields, with exactly one yes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Multiplying every term of the first equation by negative three produces the second equation. A whole nondegenerate line of points therefore satisfies both.

records.worked_problem: Solve the system $4x-2y=6$, $6x-3y=3$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Distinguishes a false numeric result from identity only after recognizing the equations as nondegenerate line conditions.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Scaling produces 12x-6y=18 and 12x-6y=6; subtraction yields false 0=12, so no solution.

records.canonical_objective: Detect special cases from slopes and graphs
records.canonical_constraints: parallel -> none; same line -> infinitely many; else one

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Read the graph geometry of $y=2x+5$ and $y=2x-1$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Both slopes are two, while the vertical intercepts are five and negative one. The lines are parallel and six vertical units apart, so they never intersect.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Compare slopes and intercepts of $y=-x+6$ and $2y=-2x+12$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide the second equation by two. Both graphs then have slope negative one and vertical intercept six; they coincide, with every point shared.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Compare the vertical and sloping graphs $x=5$ and $y=3x-2$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first graph is vertical. Substituting its fixed horizontal coordinate in the second gives height thirteen, so there is exactly one crossing at (5,13).

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Interpret the graphs $2x+y=9$ and $y=4$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first line has slope negative two; the second is horizontal. Their directions differ, and substituting height four gives one horizontal coordinate, five halves.

records.worked_problem: Classify the graphs of (a) $y=-4x+9$ and $y=-4x+5$; (b) $y=2x+1$ and $2y=4x+2$; (c) $x=3$ and $y=x-2$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Covers parallel, coincident, unique-slope, distinct-vertical, and vertical/nonvertical graphical cases.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: The examples yield: equal slopes/different intercepts none; identical equations infinite; x=3 with y=x-2 gives the unique point (3,1).

records.canonical_constraints: mix all three cases across generated problems

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $2x+y=3$ and $x-y=6$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Adding eliminates the vertical coordinate and gives three times the horizontal coordinate equal to nine. This fixes one pair, (3,-3), so the solution is unique.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $y=4x-7$ and $2y=8x-10$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Halve the second equation. Its slope is four with intercept negative five; the first intercept is negative seven. Equal slopes and unequal intercepts give no intersection.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $x/2+y=3$ and $x+2y=6$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Double every term of the first equation to obtain the second. The two equations impose the same line condition, leaving infinitely many possible points.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify algebraically $x=2y-5$ and $3x+y=13$. Classify the solution set: report one and infinite as yes/no fields. Here one means exactly one solution. Both no means no solutions; both yes is invalid.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Substitute the first expression for the horizontal coordinate in the second. Seven times the vertical coordinate equals twenty-eight, giving the unique pair (3,4).

records.worked_problem: Classify $5x+y=12$ and $10x+2y=19$ algebraically.
records.semantic_reasoning: Classifies all three solution-count outcomes algebraically and checks the classification against the source equations.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Twice 5x+y=12 gives right side 24, unlike 19; cancellation yields 0=5, so none.

records.canonical_objective: Check a point against both inequalities
records.canonical_constraints: the point must satisfy BOTH inequalities

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Check $(1,2)$ against $y>x$ and $y<=-x+4$. Report residuals as the ordered pair of left-side-minus-right-side differences for each inequality after substitution; report solution as yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first difference is positive one, so the strict lower condition holds. The second difference is negative one, so the inclusive upper condition holds too.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Check $(2,3)$ against $2x+y<7$ and $y>=x-2$. Report residuals as the ordered pair of left-side-minus-right-side differences for each inequality after substitution; report solution as yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first left side reaches the boundary value seven. A strict inequality excludes that boundary, even though the second difference is positive and satisfies its condition.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Check $(-1,4)$ against $-2y<=x-3$ and $y<x+7$. Report residuals as the ordered pair of left-side-minus-right-side differences for each inequality after substitution; report solution as yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first difference is negative four, which meets its nonpositive condition. The second difference is negative two, which meets the strict negative condition.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Check $(3,-1)$ against $x-2y>=6$ and $y<=2x+1$. Report residuals as the ordered pair of left-side-minus-right-side differences for each inequality after substitution; report solution as yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first left side is five, short of the required six. Its negative difference fails the nonnegative condition, so the overlap excludes this point despite the second passing.

records.worked_problem: Is $(-2, 3)$ a solution of the system $y \ge 2x-1$ and $y < x+6$?
records.semantic_reasoning: Requires a candidate to satisfy every inequality in the intersection, including strict boundary rejection.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: At (-2,3), 3>=-5 and 3<4 are both true, so the point is in the intersection.

records.canonical_objective: Boundary styles and the overlap region
records.canonical_constraints: one strict and one inclusive inequality per problem

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For $y<=2x+3$ and $y>-x+1$, Describe the overlap by reporting solid and dashed as (m,c,d) for boundary lines in y=mx+c form. Direction d is 1 for shading above and -1 for shading below. Include the solid boundary and exclude the dashed boundary. The solution is the intersection of those two half-planes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The inclusive first inequality has a solid boundary with slope two and intercept three, shading below. The strict second has slope negative one and intercept one, shading above.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For $y<3x-2$ and $y>=x+4$, Describe the overlap by reporting solid and dashed as (m,c,d) for boundary lines in y=mx+c form. Direction d is 1 for shading above and -1 for shading below. Include the solid boundary and exclude the dashed boundary. The solution is the intersection of those two half-planes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The second inequality supplies the solid boundary, slope one and intercept four, with shading above. The first supplies the dashed boundary, slope three and intercept negative two, shading below.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For $-2y<=4x-6$ and $3y>3x+12$, Describe the overlap by reporting solid and dashed as (m,c,d) for boundary lines in y=mx+c form. Direction d is 1 for shading above and -1 for shading below. Include the solid boundary and exclude the dashed boundary. The solution is the intersection of those two half-planes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide the first inequality by negative two and reverse its direction: shade above its solid line with slope negative two and intercept three. Divide the second by three; shade above its dashed line.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For $x+2y>=8$ and $-y>x-5$, Describe the overlap by reporting solid and dashed as (m,c,d) for boundary lines in y=mx+c form. Direction d is 1 for shading above and -1 for shading below. Include the solid boundary and exclude the dashed boundary. The solution is the intersection of those two half-planes.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Isolate height in the first: its solid line has slope negative one half and intercept four, with shading above. Negative division in the second reverses direction, shading below its dashed line.

records.worked_problem: Describe the overlap of $y\ge x-3$ and $y<-2x+6$, including boundary styles.
records.semantic_reasoning: Combines correct solid/dashed boundaries with independent half-plane directions and all possible overlap geometries, including empty.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: The overlap is x-3<=y<-2x+6; (0,0) satisfies 0>=-3 and 0<6.

records.canonical_objective: Locate a point in the solution region
records.canonical_constraints: candidate points off the boundary lines

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Which of $(1,3)$ or $(2,1)$ belongs to the overlap of $y>x+1$ and $y<x+5$? Give the ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: At the first candidate the height exceeds the lower line by one and is three below the upper line. The second candidate lies below its lower bound, so only the first is in the strip.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Which of $(0,7)$ or $(2,3)$ belongs to the overlap of $x+y<6$ and $y>=x$? Give the ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first candidate has coordinate sum seven, so it fails the strict upper condition. The second has sum five and height three above horizontal coordinate two, so it meets both conditions.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Which of $(-1,3)$ or $(1,-2)$ belongs to the overlap of $-2y<x$ and $y<=x+6$? Give the ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: For the first point, negative six is less than negative one and three is at most five. For the second, four is not less than one, so it fails the strict condition.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Which of $(3,6)$ or $(2,4)$ belongs to the overlap of $y>2x-1$ and $y<-x+8$? Give the ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The first point fails the upper bound because six exceeds five. The second height is above three and below six, so it satisfies both strict inequalities.

records.worked_problem: Which of $(3, 10)$ or $(3, -4)$ satisfies both $y > 2x+1$ and $y < 5x-2$?
records.semantic_reasoning: Tests each candidate against both inequalities and retains only a point in the overlap.

records.canonical_constraints: one count equation and one value equation

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Adult and child tickets have values 9 and 4 euros, respectively. There are 17 items with total value 108 euros. Find the counts (first type, second type).
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=17$ and $9x+4y=108$. Subtract 4 times the count equation: $5x=40$. Thus $x=8$, $y=9$. Check: $8+9=17$ and $9(8)+4(9)=108$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Five-cent and twenty-cent coins have values 5 and 20 cents, respectively. There are 13 items with total value 155 cents. Find the counts (first type, second type).
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=13$ and $5x+20y=155$. Subtract 20 times the count equation: $-15x=-105$. Thus $x=7$, $y=6$. Check: $7+6=13$ and $5(7)+20(6)=155$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Large and small meal vouchers have values 12 and 7 euros, respectively. There are 19 items with total value 173 euros. Find the counts (first type, second type).
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=19$ and $12x+7y=173$. Subtract 7 times the count equation: $5x=40$. Thus $x=8$, $y=11$. Check: $8+11=19$ and $12(8)+7(11)=173$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Standard and premium tokens have values 6 and 15 euros, respectively. There are 11 items with total value 138 euros. Find the counts (first type, second type).
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=11$ and $6x+15y=138$. Subtract 15 times the count equation: $-9x=-27$. Thus $x=3$, $y=8$. Check: $3+8=11$ and $6(3)+15(8)=138$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

records.worked_problem: Pens cost €3 and erasers cost €2. Twenty-five items sold for €63. How many of each?
records.semantic_reasoning: Pairs one total-count equation with one total-value equation and demonstrates solving for both item counts.

records.canonical_constraints: two purchases of the same two items; elimination-friendly numbers

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Pens and notebooks have fixed unit prices. Buying 3 of the first and 2 of the second costs 29 euros; buying 1 of the first and 2 of the second costs 15 euros. Find the unit prices (first, second) in euros.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ be the requested prices. Then $3x+2y=29$ and $1x+2y=15$. Multiply the first equation by 1 and the second by -3; adding gives $-4y=-16$. Recover $x=7$, $y=4$. Check: $3(7)+2(4)=29$ and $1(7)+2(4)=15$. Both prices are positive.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Sandwiches and drinks have fixed unit prices. Buying 2 of the first and 1 of the second costs 17 euros; buying 1 of the first and 3 of the second costs 26 euros. Find the unit prices (first, second) in euros.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ be the requested prices. Then $2x+1y=17$ and $1x+3y=26$. Multiply the first equation by 1 and the second by -2; adding gives $-5y=-35$. Recover $x=5$, $y=7$. Check: $2(5)+1(7)=17$ and $1(5)+3(7)=26$. Both prices are positive.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Apples and pears have fixed unit prices. Buying 1 of the first and 4 of the second costs 23 euros; buying 3 of the first and 2 of the second costs 29 euros. Find the unit prices (first, second) in euros.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ be the requested prices. Then $1x+4y=23$ and $3x+2y=29$. Multiply the first equation by 3 and the second by -1; adding gives $10y=40$. Recover $x=7$, $y=4$. Check: $1(7)+4(4)=23$ and $3(7)+2(4)=29$. Both prices are positive.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Coffees and buns have fixed unit prices. Buying 4 of the first and 3 of the second costs 47 euros; buying 2 of the first and 1 of the second costs 21 euros. Find the unit prices (first, second) in euros.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ be the requested prices. Then $4x+3y=47$ and $2x+1y=21$. Multiply the first equation by 2 and the second by -4; adding gives $2y=10$. Recover $x=8$, $y=5$. Check: $4(8)+3(5)=47$ and $2(8)+1(5)=21$. Both prices are positive.

records.worked_problem: Four pads and one marker cost EUR $26$; two pads and three markers cost EUR $28$. Find each unit price by elimination.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses stable item prices across two purchases, eliminates one price, reports units, and checks both transactions.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: 4p+m=26 and 2p+3m=28 give m=6,p=5; both totals recompute to 26 and 28.

records.canonical_constraints: verify counts are nonnegative integers and totals match

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Adult and child tickets have values 11 and 5 euros, respectively. There are 24 items with total value 174 euros. How many of the first type are there? Verify both totals.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=24$ and $11x+5y=174$. Subtract 5 times the count equation: $6x=54$. Thus $x=9$, $y=15$. Check: $9+15=24$ and $11(9)+5(15)=174$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Twenty-five-cent and ten-cent coins have values 25 and 10 cents, respectively. There are 18 items with total value 285 cents. How many of the first type are there? Verify both totals.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=18$ and $25x+10y=285$. Subtract 10 times the count equation: $15x=105$. Thus $x=7$, $y=11$. Check: $7+11=18$ and $25(7)+10(11)=285$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Full-price and discount coupons have values 8 and 3 euros, respectively. There are 16 items with total value 48 euros. How many of the first type are there? Verify both totals.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count full-price and discount coupons. Then $x+y=16$ and $8x+3y=48$. Subtract three times the count equation to get $5x=0$, hence $x=0$ and $y=16$. Check: all sixteen coupons are discounted, giving $3*16=48$ euros. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Basic and deluxe tokens have values 4 and 9 euros, respectively. There are 23 items with total value 147 euros. How many of the first type are there? Verify both totals.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ count the types in the stated order. Then $x+y=23$ and $4x+9y=147$. Subtract 9 times the count equation: $-5x=-60$. Thus $x=12$, $y=11$. Check: $12+11=23$ and $4(12)+9(11)=147$. Both counts are nonnegative integers.

records.worked_problem: A club sells $30$ tickets. Each standard ticket costs EUR $6$ and each premium ticket EUR $14$. Total revenue is EUR $260$. Find both counts and verify them.
records.semantic_reasoning: Checks nonnegative integer counts as well as count and value totals, including a permitted zero-count boundary.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: With p premium, 6(30-p)+14p=260 gives p=10 and standard=20; counts total 30 and revenue 260.

records.canonical_objective: Set up the amount and value equations
records.canonical_constraints: amount equation plus concentration (pure-substance) equation

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Blend 10% and 50% acid into 16 liters at 25%. Let x and y be the amounts of the first and second ingredients. Complete $x+y=T$ and $px+qy=M$ by giving $(T,p,q,M)$; p and q are pure-substance fractions, and M is the pure amount.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The liquid amounts sum to 16. Pure acid is one tenth of the first and one half of the second; the target holds $16(1/4)=4$ liters of acid.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Dilute pure acid (100%) with water (0%) into 9 liters at 40%. Let x and y be the amounts of the first and second ingredients. Complete $x+y=T$ and $px+qy=M$ by giving $(T,p,q,M)$; p and q are pure-substance fractions, and M is the pure amount.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Water contributes liquid but no acid. The pure ingredient contributes its full amount; the target acid amount is $9(2/5)=18/5$ liters.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Combine solutions with pure fractions 1/4 and 3/4 into 14 liters with pure fraction 3/7. Let x and y be the amounts of the first and second ingredients. Complete $x+y=T$ and $px+qy=M$ by giving $(T,p,q,M)$; p and q are pure-substance fractions, and M is the pure amount.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Use 14 as the total volume. The ingredient fractions multiply their volumes; the target pure volume is $14(3/7)=6$ liters.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Blend 30% and 80% solutions into 20 liters containing 11 liters of pure substance. Let x and y be the amounts of the first and second ingredients. Complete $x+y=T$ and $px+qy=M$ by giving $(T,p,q,M)$; p and q are pure-substance fractions, and M is the pure amount.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The total-volume equation uses 20. Convert 30% and 80% to fractional multipliers; the pure-volume equation uses the stated 11 liters.

records.worked_problem: In a model where volumes add, mix $x$ L of $10\%$ dye solution with $y$ L of $90\%$ dye solution to obtain $50$ L at $42\%$. Write both equations.
records.semantic_reasoning: States the additive-amount assumption, total equation, pure-substance balance, target calculation, and unit conversion.

records.canonical_constraints: target strength strictly between the two ingredient strengths

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Blend 10% and 40% acid into 18 liters at 20%. Give the amounts (first, second) in liters; assume volumes add.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Use $x+y=18$ and $x+4y=36$ after scaling the acid balance. Subtraction gives $3y=18$. Check: $12+6=18$ and $12+4(6)=36$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Dilute pure acid (100%) with water (0%) into 7 liters at 30%. Give the amounts (first, second) in liters; assume volumes add.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Only the first ingredient supplies acid, so its volume is $7(3/10)=21/10$. Check: $21/10+49/10=7$ and the pure share is three tenths.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Combine solutions with pure fractions 1/5 and 4/5 into 15 liters with pure fraction 1/2. Give the amounts (first, second) in liters; assume volumes add.
Blend 25% and 75% solutions into 24 liters containing 15 liters of pure substance. Give the amounts (first, second) in liters; assume volumes add.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Use $x+y=24$ and $x+3y=60$. Subtraction gives $2y=36$. Check: $6+18=24$ and $6/4+3(18)/4=15$.

records.worked_problem: In a model where volumes add, how many litres of $5\%$ and $80\%$ dye solutions make $45$ L of $30\%$ dye solution?
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses a target strictly between ingredient strengths, solves positive amounts, and checks both volume and pure substance.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: x+y=45 and .05x+.80y=13.5 give y=15,x=30; pure amounts 1.5+12=13.5.

records.canonical_constraints: blend price between the two ingredient prices; halves allowed

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Blend tea priced at 6 and 14 euros/kg into 12 kilograms worth 9 euros/kg. Give the masses (first, second) in kilograms; assume no loss.
Combine nuts priced at 8 and 20 euros/kg into 10 kilograms with total value 128 euros. Give the masses (first, second) in kilograms; assume no loss.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The total value is already supplied: $8x+20y=128$ with $x+y=10$. Check: $6+4=10$ and $8(6)+20(4)=128$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Mix coffee priced at 1600 and 1000 cents/kg into 9 kilograms worth 12 euros/kg. Give the masses (first, second) in kilograms; assume no loss.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Convert the prices to 16 and 10 euros/kg. Use $x+y=9$ and $16x+10y=108$. Check: $3+6=9$ and $16(3)+10(6)=108$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Blend grain priced at 4 and 10 euros/kg into 8000 grams worth 7 euros/kg. Give the masses (first, second) in kilograms; assume no loss.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Convert the total mass to 8 kilograms. Use $x+y=8$ and $4x+10y=56$. Check: $4+4=8$ and $4(4)+10(4)=56$.

records.worked_problem: Tea at €4/kg is blended with tea at €20/kg to make $16$ kg worth €10/kg. How much of each?
records.semantic_reasoning: Builds mass and value equations with consistent mass/currency units and verifies the blend value.

records.canonical_objective: Current and wind: sum and difference
records.canonical_constraints: downstream = sum, upstream = difference of the two rates

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A boat maintains a constant still-medium speed. Its ground speeds are 18 km/h with the current or wind and 10 km/h against it. Find (still-medium speed, current or wind speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ be the requested speeds. Then $x+y=18$ and $x-y=10$. Add: $2x=28$; subtract: $2y=8$. Thus $x=14$ and $y=4$. Check: $14+4=18$ and $14-4=10$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A flight log records ground speeds of 420 km/h against a steady wind and 540 km/h with it. The plane keeps the same airspeed. Find (airspeed, wind speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Let $x,y$ be the requested speeds. Then $x+y=540$ and $x-y=420$. Add: $2x=960$; subtract: $2y=120$. Thus $x=480$ and $y=60$. Check: $480+60=540$ and $480-60=420$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A kayak maintains the same paddling effort. Its ground speeds are 200 metres/min with the current and 150 metres/min against it. Find (still-water speed, current speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Convert to km/h: $200*60/1000=12$ and $150*60/1000=9$. Let $x,y$ be still-water and current speeds. Then $x+y=12$ and $x-y=9$. Adding gives $2x=21$, so $x=21/2$ and $y=3/2$. Check: $21/2+3/2=12$ and $21/2-3/2=9$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A ferry runs at 37 km/h downstream and 25 km/h upstream. A learner uses the full difference as the current speed. Correct the calculation and give (still-water speed, current speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The difference includes the current effect twice: $2y=37-25=12$. Thus $y=6$. The sum gives $2x=37+25=62$, hence $x=31$. Check: $31+6=37$ and $31-6=25$.

records.worked_problem: A boat travels straight along a steady current at $21$ km/h downstream and $15$ km/h upstream, maintaining the same speed relative to the water. Find that still-water speed and the current speed.
records.semantic_reasoning: States the equal relative-speed and steady-medium assumptions and uses sum/difference ground-speed equations in matched units.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: b+c=21 and b-c=15 give 2b=36 and 2c=6, so b=18,c=3.

records.canonical_objective: Compute the two speeds from d = rt first
records.canonical_constraints: distances divide evenly by the times

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A canoe travels 42 km in 2 h with the current or wind and 42 km in 3 h against it. Its still-medium speed and the current or wind stay constant. Find (still-medium speed, current or wind speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide distance by time first: $42/2=21$ and $42/3=14$. Then $x+y=21$ and $x-y=14$. Add and halve to get $x=35/2$; subtract and halve to get $y=7/2$. Check: $(35/2+7/2)*2=42$ and $(35/2-7/2)*3=42$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A plane travels 1800 km in 3 h with the current or wind and 2000 km in 4 h against it. Its still-medium speed and the current or wind stay constant. Find (still-medium speed, current or wind speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide distance by time first: $1800/3=600$ and $2000/4=500$. Then $x+y=600$ and $x-y=500$. Add and halve to get $x=550$; subtract and halve to get $y=50$. Check: $(550+50)*3=1800$ and $(550-50)*4=2000$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A launch travels 60 km in 180 minutes downstream and 48 km in 240 minutes upstream. Its still-water speed and the current stay constant. Find (still-water speed, current speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Convert minutes to hours: $180/60=3$ and $240/60=4$. Ground speeds are $60/3=20$ and $48/4=12$. Use $x+y=20$ and $x-y=12$ to get $x=16$ and $y=4$. Check: $(16+4)*3=60$ and $(16-4)*4=48$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A ferry log lists an upstream leg of 45 km taking 3 h and a downstream leg of 35 km taking 1 h. Its still-water speed and the current stay constant. Find (still-water speed, current speed) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide distance by time first: $35/1=35$ and $45/3=15$. Then $x+y=35$ and $x-y=15$. Add and halve to get $x=25$; subtract and halve to get $y=10$. Check: $(25+10)*1=35$ and $(25-10)*3=45$.

records.worked_problem: A rowing team covers $40$ km downstream in $4$ h and $40$ km upstream in $5$ h. Find the rowing speed and the current speed.
records.semantic_reasoning: Computes each ground speed from distance and time before forming sum/difference equations and checking original distances.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Ground speeds are 40/4=10 and 40/5=8; sum/difference give rowing=9,current=1.

records.canonical_constraints: meeting problems: combined speed = total distance / time

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Two cars start 420 km apart and travel toward each other at constant speeds, meeting after 3 h. The faster speed exceeds the slower by 12 km/h. Find (faster, slower) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The combined speed is $420/3=140$. With faster $x$, slower $y$, use $x+y=140$ and $x-y=12$. Add and halve to obtain $x=76$; then $y=64$. Check: $(76+64)*3=420$ and $76-64=12$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Two trains start 660 km apart and move toward each other at constant speeds, meeting after 6 h. The faster train covers 108 km more than the slower during those 6 h. Find (faster, slower) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Combined speed is $660/6=110$; the speed difference is $108/6=18$. Use $x+y=110$ and $x-y=18$ to get $x=64$ and $y=46$. Check: $(64+46)*6=660$ and $(64-46)*6=108$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Two cyclists start 99 km apart and travel toward each other at constant speeds, meeting after 180 minutes. The faster speed exceeds the slower by 5 km/h. Find (faster, slower) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Convert time: $180/60=3$ hours. Combined speed is $99/3=33$. Then $x+y=33$ and $x-y=5$, so $x=19$ and $y=14$. Check: $(19+14)*3=99$ and $19-14=5$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Two walkers start 46 km apart and travel toward each other at constant speeds, meeting after 4 h. The faster speed is 25/21 times the slower speed. Find (faster, slower) in km/h.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Combined speed is $46/4=23/2$. With faster $x$, slower $y$, use $x+y=23/2$ and $21x=25y$. Substitute to get $46y/21=23/2$, hence $y=21/4$ and $x=25/4$. Check: $(25/4+21/4)*4=46$ and $21*(25/4)=25*(21/4)$.

records.worked_problem: Two hikers start $56$ km apart on a trail and walk toward each other, meeting after $7$ h. One hikes $2$ km/h faster than the other. Find both speeds.
records.semantic_reasoning: Derives combined speed from separation and meeting time, then uses an independent difference or ratio relation.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Combined speed=56/7=8 and difference=2; solving gives faster=5, slower=3.

limitations: Semantic review only. Receipts are rebound to the post-repairs curriculum snapshot after exact diff review. Production gates were outside this review; no proposal files or live content were modified.
